extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, history, and public policy
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of standing armies and justice
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and evaluation of how military organization (standing armies vs. militias) and the administration of justice arise, operate, and affect civil society and public expense across stages of social development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of a well regulated standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: A well regulated standing army is superior to every militia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that a disciplined standing army, maintained by an opulent and civilized nation, is generally superior to militias (both civilized and barbarous) in battle and in defending civilization; examples include Hannibal's standing troops vs Roman militia and later Roman standing armies subduing militias of Greece, Syria, and Egypt. The standing army also allows a civilized nation to defend itself against poorer, barbarous neighbours and helps perpetuate civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing army as instrument of internal order and civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing army establishes, with an irresistible force, the law of the sovereign through the remotest provinces of the empire, and maintains some degree of regular government in countries which could not otherwise admit of any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith uses Peter the Great's reforms in Russia as an example: many improvements in that empire resolved themselves into establishing a well regulated standing army, which executed and maintained other regulations and produced order and internal peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk to liberty from standing armies unless interests aligned
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of republican principles have been jealous of a standing army, as dangerous to liberty. It certainly is so, wherever the interest of the general, and that of the principal officers, are not necessarily connected with the support of the constitution of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing armies have overthrown republics (Caesar) or upset parliaments (Cromwell) when military leaders' interests diverge from civil institutions. Conversely, if the sovereign is the general and principal nobility/gentry are chief officers — i.e., when military command is held by those with the greatest stake in civil authority — a standing army is less dangerous and may even favor liberty by stabilizing government and reducing destabilizing popular jealousies.

rubrics_metrics.name: First duty of the sovereign: external defense becomes costlier with civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The first duty of the sovereign, that of defending the society from the violence and injustice of other independent societies, grows gradually more and more expensive, as the society advances in civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As societies improve, maintaining military force — initially no cost when militia sufficed — comes to require maintenance by the sovereign in war and later in peace. The invention of firearms and more complex artillery further enhances expense of exercising, disciplining, and employing soldiers and fortifying towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firearms revolution increases military expense and advantages the wealthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The great change introduced into the art of war by the invention of fire-arms, has enhanced still further both the expense of exercising and disciplining any particular number of soldiers in time of peace, and that of employing them in time of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firearms (muskets, cannon, powder) are more expensive and heavier than ancient arms (javelins, bows, catapults), increasing costs for training, ammunition (which is irrecoverable), transport, and fortification. Consequently, modern warfare gives an advantage to nations that can better afford these expenses — opulent and civilized nations over poor and barbarous ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia vs standing army dynamics: experience and discipline matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Militia opposed to a standing army are at a disadvantage; long service in the field forms a militia into a standing army with superior discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Carthaginian troops who had been continually in the field under consistent generals were better disciplined than Roman militias at Trebi, Trasimene, and Cannae. Conversely, Roman militias, being frequently mobilized, became better disciplined over time (e.g., Scipio’s forces). Thus continual field service and consistent command are crucial to creating an effective army.

rubrics_metrics.name: External adoption creates security imperative for standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: When the expedient of a standing army has once been adopted by one civilized nation, it became necessary that all its neighbours should follow the example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States adopt standing armies not only for intrinsic advantages but because neighbours’ adoption creates a security externality: safety depends on following suit, as militia alone becomes incapable of resisting such armies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long peace may relax generals' skill but preserves soldiers' valour in regulated armies
rubrics_metrics.description: In a long peace, the generals, perhaps, may sometimes forget their skill; but where a well regulated standing army has been kept up, the soldiers seem never to forget their valour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith cites the Russian army (after long peace) and English soldiers (after 28 years peace before the Spanish war) to argue that well-regulated standing armies retain soldierly courage even without recent combat experience, though officer skill may atrophy without active command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense and form of administration of justice depends on stage of society
rubrics_metrics.description: The second duty of the sovereign, that of establishing an exact administration of justice, requires two very different degrees of expense in the different periods of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among hunter societies with little property, regular magistrates and courts are uncommon; as valuable property emerges, the need for magistracy and a more costly justice system increases. Thus the expense of justice rises with property accumulation and societal complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil government is required to secure valuable property
rubrics_metrics.description: The acquisition of valuable and extensive property necessarily requires the establishment of civil government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where property exceeds trivial values, owners are vulnerable to theft or expropriation; protecting accumulated property (often resulting from many years or generations of labour) requires a civil magistrate and continual enforcement — otherwise owners cannot securely enjoy the fruits of their labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four natural causes of subordination (foundations for civil authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes or circumstances which naturally introduce subordination ... seem to be four in number: (1) superiority of personal qualifications, (2) superiority of age, (3) superiority of fortune, (4) superiority of birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith explains each: personal qualities (strength, wisdom) can give authority though invisible and disputable; age is plain and admitted universally; fortune creates economic dependence and command; birth (ancestral wealth and antiquity) confers respect and established precedence — together these foster rank, subordination, and early forms of civil government.

rubrics_metrics.name: In societies with inequality, civil government serves to protect the rich against the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil government, so far as it is instituted for the security of property, is, in reality, instituted for the defence of the rich against the poor, or of those who have some property against those who have none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As inequalities of fortune arise (especially in shepherd societies), the wealthy naturally seek protection of their property and authority; lesser landholders support greater ones because their own security depends on that higher authority, creating a mutual interest in sustaining civil government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of justice as a revenue source fosters corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration of justice not only afforded a certain revenue to the sovereign, but, to procure this revenue, seems to have been one of the principal advantages which he proposed to obtain by the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When justice is monetized through presents, fees, and amercements, abuses follow: richer petitioners get better outcomes, delays occur to extract repeated presents, and officials may find incentive to rule wrongly to collect amercements. Historical circuit-judge practices under Henry II illustrate judges acting as itinerant factors to levy revenue, producing gross abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of judicial authority risks extension of abuses for sovereign benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: When the sovereign or chief exercises his judicial authority by a bailiff, if the bailiff acts for the benefit of his sovereign, redress is often impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegating justice to bailiffs/judges can allow oppressive acts to persist if those acts serve the sovereign's interests; while some abuses could be checked if bailiffs acted for personal gain only, state-motivated corruption is harder to remedy, especially in barbarous governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition to public taxation often involves eliminating judicial presents
rubrics_metrics.description: When the private estate of the sovereign had become altogether insufficient for defraying the expense of the sovereignty... it seems to have been very commonly stipulated, that no present for the administration of justice should, under any pretence, be accepted either by the sovereign, or by his bailiffs and substitutes, the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As states move from sovereign-funded to taxpayer-funded defense and administration, a common reform was to abolish judicial presents/fees — seen as easier to abolish outright than to regulate precisely — to reduce corruption associated with monetizing justice.
